content: Avian influenza, commonly referred to as bird flu, is an infectious disease caused by a virus that primarily affects wild and domestic birds. Wild birds, particularly migratory waterfowl such as ducks, geese, and swans, as well as shorebirds like storks, are natural carriers of bird flu viruses. These viruses can be transmitted from wild birds to domestic poultry, including chickens, turkeys, geese, and pheasants. The virus is present in the feces of infected birds, as well as in secretions from their eyes, noses, or mouths. Although bird flu viruses do not typically infect humans, transmission can occur under certain circumstances. Individuals may become infected if they touch their eyes, nose, or mouth after handling infected live or dead birds, or after coming into contact with surfaces or objects contaminated with the virus. Inhalation of virus-laden droplets or dust can also lead to infection. The clinical presentation of bird flu in humans can range from asymptomatic cases to severe illness. Mild symptoms may include conjunctivitis (redness of the eyes), cough, sore throat, nasal congestion or discharge, muscle aches, headaches, and fatigue. Severe cases may present with high fever, shortness of breath, and difficulty breathing. In some instances, severe disease can progress to pneumonia, necessitating hospitalization. Less commonly, symptoms such as diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, or seizures may occur. For travelers, the risk of contracting bird flu is generally low. To minimize the risk of bird flu infection, travelers should adhere to the following precautions: Avoid direct contact with birds and refrain from visiting areas where birds are housed, such as poultry farms, live-animal markets, or facilities where birds are raised, slaughtered, or sold. If visiting such locations is unavoidable, wear a properly fitted face mask and avoid handling birds or poultry. Do not touch sick or dead wild birds or poultry. Wash hands frequently with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially after contact with birds, bird habitats, or raw poultry. If soap and water are unavailable, use a hand sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol. Avoid touching the eyes, nose, or mouth. Refrain from close physical contact, such as kissing, hugging, or sharing eating utensils or drinking vessels, with individuals who are ill.
